lessons.title: The five I/O models
lessons.summary: Blocking, non-blocking, multiplexed, signal-driven and asynchronous I/O as Stevens classified them, readiness versus completion, and what "async" actually means.
lessons.body:
When a program asks to read from a socket, the data may not have arrived yet. What should happen? The program could wait, could be told "try again", could ask to be notified, or could ask the kernel to finish the whole job in the background.

W. Richard Stevens, in *Unix Network Programming*, sorted the options into **five I/O models**. They are still the clearest way to think about every server framework you will meet, from Apache to Node.js to io_uring.

## A two-phase model of ordinary socket input

For an ordinary buffered socket read, use this simplified two-phase model:

1. **Wait for the data to be ready.** For a socket, a packet must arrive and land in the kernel's receive buffer.
2. **Copy the data from kernel to user space.** The kernel copies bytes from its buffer into the buffer you passed to `read()` or `recv()`.

Phase 1 can take forever (a client that never sends). Phase 2 involves copying with a cost dependent on size, memory state and implementation; it has no fixed microsecond duration. The five models differ in how the process experiences each phase.

```
   app             kernel
    |   read()  -->  | no data yet
    |                |   ... wait ...  (1)
    |                | data arrives
    |                | copy to user    (2)
    |  <-- n bytes   |
```

## 1. Blocking I/O

For a blocking stream socket, a positive-length `read()` can wait for data, EOF or an error. Available data may return immediately, possibly as a short read; copying is completed before the call returns.

```c
char buf[4096];
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
/* n > 0: got n bytes
   n == 0: peer closed (EOF)
   n < 0: error, see errno */
```

Blocking I/O is simple and efficient for one stream: the thread uses no CPU while asleep. The trouble starts with many streams. A thread blocked on client A cannot notice that client B has sent something.

The classic answer is **one thread (or process) per connection**, as in Apache's prefork and worker models. Its costs depend on the workload and resource limits:

- Each thread needs a stack (size determined by thread attributes and runtime limits, not a universal Linux 8 MB default; reserved address space differs from resident memory) and a kernel task structure.
- Runnable threads and wakeups add scheduler work; idle sleeping threads mainly consume memory and bookkeeping resources.
- Most of those threads are just asleep, waiting for slow clients.

## 2. Non-blocking I/O

Set `O_NONBLOCK` on the descriptor and `read()` never sleeps in phase 1. For supported socket operations with no available data, EOF or other result, it reports `EAGAIN` or `EWOULDBLOCK`. Portable code checks both; these constants need not be equal on every platform.

```c
int fl = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
if (fl == -1) {
    perror("F_GETFL"); exit(1);
}
if (fcntl(fd, F_SETFL,
          fl | O_NONBLOCK) == -1) {
    perror("F_SETFL"); exit(1);
}

ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
if (n < 0 && (errno == EAGAIN ||
              errno == EWOULDBLOCK)) {
    /* nothing yet: do other work */
}
```

The Python equivalent raises `BlockingIOError`:

```python
import socket

s = socket.create_connection(
    ("example.com", 80))
s.setblocking(False)
try:
    data = s.recv(4096)
except BlockingIOError:
    data = None   # EAGAIN: try later
```

A naive use of non-blocking I/O can lead to **busy-polling**: loop over every socket calling `read()`, getting `EAGAIN` from almost all of them, burning CPU. Its real value is as a building block for model 3.

Note that phase 2 is still synchronous. When data *is* ready, `read()` copies it before returning.

> [!warning] O_NONBLOCK does nothing for regular files
> On Linux, `O_NONBLOCK` is ignored for regular files and block devices. A `read()` that misses the page cache blocks for the disk regardless. select and poll always report regular files as ready, and epoll refuses them outright with `EPERM`. This is why Node.js runs file operations on a thread pool (lesson 5).

## 3. I/O multiplexing

Instead of blocking in `read()` on one descriptor, block in a call that watches **many** descriptors and returns when any is ready: `select`, `poll`, `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on BSD and macOS.

```
select/epoll_wait  --> blocks (phase 1)
   returns "fd 7 is readable"
read(7)            --> copies (phase 2)
```

One thread can now serve tens of thousands of connections. This is the foundation of nginx, Redis, Node.js and Python's `asyncio`. The next lesson covers these calls in detail.

Multiplexing tells you about **readiness**: "a read on fd 7 will not block now". You still do the I/O yourself. Descriptors are normally also set non-blocking, because readiness can become stale or be spurious. An ordinary stream read need not wait to fill its buffer, but flags such as MSG_WAITALL and concurrent readers require care.

## 4. Signal-driven I/O

Ask the kernel to send a `SIGIO` signal when a descriptor becomes ready:

```c
signal(SIGIO, on_sigio);
fcntl(fd, F_SETOWN, getpid());
int fl = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, fl | O_ASYNC);
```

The process carries on running; the signal handler (or a main loop it nudges) then calls `read()`. Phase 1 doesn't block; phase 2 still does.

Standard SIGIO notifications can coalesce, so programs must re-check descriptor state rather than count signals as events. Signal handlers have async-signal-safety restrictions. Linux `F_SETSIG` with `SA_SIGINFO` can include descriptor/event information, and real-time signals can queue subject to resource limits; fallback to SIGIO is possible. Multiplexing often makes per-descriptor event handling easier.

## 5. Asynchronous I/O

Request "read into this buffer and report when it is **done**". A completion interface separates submission from collecting the result. The operation may finish before submission returns or later, and the implementation may use kernel machinery or helper threads. Submission itself still has cost and possible errors.

POSIX defines `aio_read` for this:

```c
struct aiocb cb = {0};
cb.aio_fildes = fd;
cb.aio_buf    = buf;
cb.aio_nbytes = sizeof buf;
cb.aio_offset = 0;
cb.aio_sigevent.sigev_notify = SIGEV_NONE;

if (aio_read(&cb) == -1) {
    perror("aio_read"); exit(1);
}
do_other_work();
while (aio_error(&cb) == EINPROGRESS)
    ;                  /* or aio_suspend */
int status = aio_error(&cb);
ssize_t n = aio_return(&cb);
/* status: completion error, or 0. */
```

The catch on Linux: glibc's POSIX AIO is implemented in user space with a pool of threads doing ordinary blocking calls. Linux native AIO (`io_submit`) has operation/filesystem limitations, and submission can block even with direct I/O in some paths. **io_uring**, introduced in Linux 5.1 in 2019, provides a broader completion interface; it can also use worker threads and has operation-specific support rules (lesson 4). Windows has had it for decades as **I/O completion ports (IOCP)**.

## The models side by side

| Model | Phase 1 (wait) | Phase 2 (copy) |
|---|---|---|
| Blocking | Blocks | Blocks |
| Non-blocking | Returns EAGAIN | Blocks |
| Multiplexing | Blocks in select | Blocks |
| Signal-driven | Signal arrives | Blocks |
| Asynchronous interface | Separate submission/completion | Implementation completes it |

Stevens' crucial observation: POSIX defines a **synchronous** I/O operation as one that blocks the requesting process until the operation completes. By that definition, the first four models are all synchronous, because the calling thread cannot use the returned result until the read finishes. Here synchronous does not mean the scheduler necessarily puts that thread to sleep during copying. Model 5 instead separates submission and completion.

## Readiness versus completion

That table boils down to two families:

- **Readiness-based** (models 2 to 4, and epoll and kqueue): the kernel says *when you can* do I/O without blocking. You then do it.
- **Completion-based** (model 5, IOCP, io_uring): you say *what* I/O to do. The kernel does it and tells you when it's *finished*.

The difference shapes everything above it:

| | Readiness | Completion |
|---|---|---|
| Buffer needed | At read time | At submit time |
| Ordinary regular files on Linux | Readiness is not storage completion | Supported operations can report completion |
| Syscall costs | Waits can cover many reads | Submission/completion can batch |
| Pattern | Reactor | Proactor |

With completion I/O you must hand over a buffer up front and keep it alive until the kernel finishes, which complicates memory management with 10,000 idle connections (io_uring's answer is provided buffer rings). With readiness I/O you can allocate the buffer only when data is actually there.

## What "async" really means

The word "async" is used for at least three different things:

1. **Asynchronous I/O interface**: completion is reported separately from submission; helper threads or kernel facilities may do the work (model 5).
2. **Non-blocking**: a call returns immediately rather than sleeping (model 2). Non-blocking is not the same as asynchronous; a non-blocking `read()` that finds data does the copy synchronously.
3. **async/await in a language**: a programming style where a function can pause at `await` and let an event loop run other tasks. On Unix, default selector-based asyncio and libuv commonly use readiness APIs for sockets, with worker mechanisms for some blocking work. Windows uses different backends: Python's default ProactorEventLoop and libuv use IOCP. Runtime version and event-loop choice matter.

For Node.js on a typical Unix libuv backend, asynchronous JavaScript APIs can sit above non-blocking socket readiness and worker-based file operations. That does not make every operation universally non-blocking or every platform use epoll; synchronous APIs and CPU-heavy callbacks can still block the event loop.

> [!tip] The question to ask
> Whenever a framework claims to be "asynchronous", ask: who is waiting, and where? Is a thread sleeping in `epoll_wait`, in a worker pool, or nowhere at all because the kernel is doing the work? The answer tells you how it will scale and where it can stall.

## Choosing a model

- **A few connections, simple code**: blocking I/O, possibly a thread per connection. Easy to reason about.
- **Thousands of mostly idle connections**: multiplexing with non-blocking sockets, in an event loop.
- **Linux workloads needing completion interfaces or batching**: evaluate supported io_uring operations against a measured baseline.
- **Implementation matters**: glibc POSIX AIO has asynchronous completion semantics even though workers perform the I/O; signal-driven designs require careful state and signal handling.

## Key takeaways
- The two-phase socket-read model separates waiting for readiness from copying; it is a teaching model, not every possible I/O path.
- In the first four models, the caller performs a read and receives its result when that call finishes. Completion interfaces separate submission from result collection.
- Readiness models (epoll, kqueue) tell you when you can act; completion models (IOCP, io_uring) tell you when the kernel has acted.
- `O_NONBLOCK` has no effect on regular files, which is why event loops use thread pools for disk I/O.
- Language async/await does not specify the underlying I/O mechanism; runtime, platform and operation determine readiness, completion or worker-based behavior.

> [!note] Deployment evidence gap
> No benchmark establishes connection-count limits, universal stack residency, copy latency or a fastest I/O model here. Numeric scenarios are assumptions; exact costs and runtime backends must be checked for the deployed version. C examples are fragments requiring headers, initialized descriptors/buffers and lifecycle cleanup. Keep asynchronous buffers/control blocks valid until completion.

## Further reading
- [read(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html)
- [fcntl(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fcntl.2.html)
- [aio(7) — POSIX asynchronous I/O overview](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/aio.7.html)
- [Asynchronous I/O — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asynchronous_I/O)
- [Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API — LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/776703/)

questions.prompt: A positive-length blocking `read()` on an established TCP socket returns `0`, with no local receive-side shutdown. What does this indicate?

options.text: No data has arrived yet; try again later
options.explanation: Absent EOF or errors, a blocking positive-length read can wait for data. In non-blocking mode an empty open stream normally reports EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK.

options.text: The peer has closed its side of the connection (end of file)
options.explanation: Correct. A return of 0 means EOF: the other side has shut down writing and no more data will arrive.

options.text: An error occurred; check `errno`
options.explanation: Errors are signalled by a return of -1. A return of 0 is a normal, successful result meaning EOF.

options.text: The buffer passed in was too small
options.explanation: A small buffer just means a short read of up to that many bytes; the remaining data stays in the kernel buffer for the next call.

questions.workedExample: For the stated positive-length stream read, a positive return reports bytes, zero indicates receive EOF, and −1 reports an error. After buffered bytes are consumed, a peer FIN produces EOF; the peer may have half-closed only its sending direction. A zero-byte read request is a different case and need not mean EOF. Do not busy-retry EOF as though it were EAGAIN.

questions.prompt:
Consider this Python snippet after a successful connection. The server keeps its sending side open, sends no data, and no reset or other error occurs.

```python
s = socket.create_connection(
    (host, port))
s.setblocking(False)
try:
    print(s.recv(100))
except BlockingIOError:
    print("later")
```

What does it print?

options.text: Nothing; it hangs until the server sends data
options.explanation: That's the behaviour of a *blocking* socket. `setblocking(False)` sets `O_NONBLOCK`, so `recv` won't sleep.
An empty bytes object means EOF (the peer closed). Here the peer is still connected, just silent.

options.text: `later`
options.explanation: Correct. With no data in the receive buffer, the non-blocking `recv` fails with `EAGAIN`, which Python raises as `BlockingIOError`.

options.text: It raises `ConnectionResetError`
options.explanation: A reset needs the peer to send an RST. An idle, open connection simply has no data yet.

questions.workedExample:
1. `create_connection` completes the TCP handshake (in blocking mode).
2. `setblocking(False)` sets `O_NONBLOCK` on the descriptor.
3. `recv(100)` checks the receive buffer: empty.
4. A blocking socket would sleep here. A non-blocking one returns -1 with `errno = EAGAIN`.
5. Python maps `EAGAIN` to `BlockingIOError`, so the `except` branch prints `later`.

questions.prompt: In Stevens' classification, which phase of a read does **I/O multiplexing** (e.g. `select`) take off the individual `read()` call?

options.text: Both phases: `select` waits for data and copies it into your buffer
options.explanation: `select` only reports readiness. You still call `read()` afterwards to copy the data.

options.text: Neither phase: it is just a faster form of blocking I/O
options.explanation: It does change things: the waiting happens once, for many descriptors, inside `select`, rather than inside each `read()`.

options.text: The copy phase: `select` copies data into the kernel so `read()` is faster
options.explanation: The data is already in the kernel when it arrives; `select` doesn't move it anywhere.

options.text: The waiting phase: the thread blocks in `select` until some descriptor is ready, then `read()` only copies
options.explanation: Correct in the simple no-race model. The readiness wait covers many descriptors, followed by a separate read. Use non-blocking I/O because readiness can change before that read.

questions.workedExample:
Phases: (1) wait for data, (2) copy kernel to user.

```
select([a,b,c]) blocks  <- phase 1
 -> b ready
read(b)          copies <- phase 2
```

The gain isn't that the copy disappears; it's that one thread waits on thousands of sockets at once.

questions.prompt: By the POSIX definition Stevens uses, why is I/O multiplexing with `epoll` classed as **synchronous** I/O, even though one thread handles thousands of connections?

options.text: Because `epoll_wait` must be called from the main thread
options.explanation: There's no such restriction, and it isn't what 'synchronous' means here.

options.text: Because the process is blocked while the data is copied from kernel to user space in `read()`
options.explanation: Correct. POSIX calls an operation synchronous if the requesting process is blocked until it completes. The copy in `read()` happens on the caller's time, so the operation is synchronous.

options.text: Because the kernel processes connections one at a time
options.explanation: The kernel handles packets for many connections concurrently; this is about who performs the I/O operation, not kernel scheduling.

options.text: Because epoll uses blocking sockets
options.explanation: Event loops normally use non-blocking sockets. Even so, the copy is performed synchronously by the caller.

questions.workedExample:
1. epoll reports readiness; a later read performs the copy and returns the result to its caller.
2. The thread can execute kernel copy instructions rather than being asleep in the scheduler; synchronous describes the operation contract.
3. Completion interfaces separate submitting an operation from learning its result.
4. They may use kernel execution or workers, and an operation can finish before submission returns.

questions.prompt: On Linux, a server sets O_NONBLOCK on an ordinary regular file, then uses read() in its event loop. Tracing shows some reads waiting for storage on page-cache misses. Why does O_NONBLOCK not prevent those waits?

options.text: `O_NONBLOCK` is ignored for regular files, so a page-cache miss blocks the loop thread while the disk is read
options.explanation: Correct. Regular files are always considered 'ready'; a read that needs the disk simply sleeps. That's why libuv and nginx push file I/O onto thread pools (or use io_uring).

options.text: `EAGAIN` is returned, but the loop retries in a tight spin
options.explanation: O_NONBLOCK does not make ordinary regular-file reads return EAGAIN on page-cache misses. Other operations or filesystem situations may produce EAGAIN, so never is too broad.

options.text: The file system locks the whole file during reads
options.explanation: Concurrent reads of a file don't take an exclusive lock that would explain this. The stall is waiting for the device.

options.text: Regular files need `O_DIRECT` to be readable from an event loop
options.explanation: O_DIRECT is not required to read a file and does not turn a synchronous read into an asynchronous operation. Direct-I/O support and behavior vary by filesystem and alignment.

questions.workedExample:
1. Linux O_NONBLOCK does not provide asynchronous page-cache-miss handling for ordinary regular-file read().
2. Readiness APIs are not storage completion notifications for those files.
3. If the event-loop thread waits for storage, unrelated callbacks wait too.
4. Move supported work to a worker pool or a suitable completion interface. Actual latency and backend support must be measured, not inferred from a generic SSD/disk range.

questions.prompt: Which interfaces can report completion separately from submitting an I/O request, regardless of whether the implementation uses kernel work or helper threads? Select all that apply.

options.text: Windows I/O completion ports (IOCP)
options.explanation: Correct. You post an overlapped read with a buffer; the kernel fills it and queues a completion packet.

options.text: Linux `epoll`
options.explanation: epoll is readiness-based: it tells you a descriptor can be read without blocking, then you call `read()` yourself.

options.text: Linux io_uring
options.explanation: Correct for submitted read/write operations. io_uring also has readiness-poll operations; a CQE must be interpreted according to its opcode and result.

options.text: BSD/macOS `kqueue` with `EVFILT_READ`
options.explanation: `EVFILT_READ` reports readiness (and how many bytes are available); you still perform the read.

options.text: POSIX `aio_read`
options.explanation: Correct in its interface: you hand over a buffer and later collect the result. (On Linux glibc implements it with threads, but the model is completion.)

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each API: do I give it a buffer up front and get told when the data is *in* the buffer?

| API | Model |
|---|---|
| IOCP | completion |
| epoll | readiness |
| io_uring | completion |
| kqueue READ | readiness |
| aio_read | completion |

Readiness APIs need a second call to do the I/O; completion APIs don't.

questions.prompt: What complicates a conventional O_ASYNC + standard SIGIO design for a TCP server?

options.text: Linux doesn't support `SIGIO` on sockets
options.explanation: Linux does support it via `F_SETOWN` and `O_ASYNC`; the problem is how useful the signal is.

options.text: It requires root privileges
options.explanation: Any process can enable `O_ASYNC` on its own descriptors.

options.text: It blocks during the wait phase, which defeats the purpose
options.explanation: It doesn't block during the wait; that's its one advantage. The process runs until the signal arrives.

options.text: Standard SIGIO notifications can coalesce, the application must re-check socket state, and signal handlers have safety restrictions
options.explanation: Correct. Linux extensions can supply descriptor/event information and queue real-time signals, but queue limits and fallback to SIGIO must still be handled.

questions.workedExample:
1. Standard SIGIO signals can coalesce; one delivered signal is not one counted socket event.
2. The application must inspect current descriptor state.
3. Handler code must obey async-signal-safety rules.
4. F_SETSIG plus SA_SIGINFO can provide descriptor/event details, and real-time signals can queue up to resource limits. Overflow can revert to SIGIO.
5. Readiness multiplexing can simplify collecting per-descriptor events, though events still require correct state handling.

questions.prompt: Assume a Linux thread-per-connection server has 20,000 threads and explicitly configures an **8 MiB** stack reservation per thread. Ignoring guard pages and other mappings, what virtual stack reservation results, and must it all be resident?

options.text: About 160 MB, all of it resident
options.explanation: 20,000 × 8 MB is 160,000 MB, not 160 MB: off by a factor of 1,000.

options.text: 156.25 GiB of virtual stack reservations; resident usage depends on touched/resident pages
options.explanation: Correct. 20,000 × 8 MiB / 1024 = 156.25 GiB. This excludes guards and other memory. Thread creation can still hit process/resource limits; address-space arithmetic does not guarantee successful creation.

options.text: 156.25 GiB, necessarily all resident immediately
options.explanation: Linux reserves stack address space lazily; pages are only backed by RAM when first touched, so idle threads use much less.

options.text: Nothing; threads share the process's stack
options.explanation: Each thread needs its own stack, because each has its own call chain.

questions.workedExample:
1. 20,000 × 8 MiB = 160,000 MiB = 156.25 GiB.
2. Reserved virtual space and physical residency differ; neither this arithmetic nor the thread count determines actual resident memory.
3. If one additionally assumes 32 KiB resident per stack, the model gives 625 MiB, but no measured stack profile is supplied.
4. Thread limits, kernel metadata, guards and wakeup patterns add costs. Event loops reduce the need for a dedicated waiting thread per connection, not all scheduling/memory costs.

questions.prompt: With CPython's default selector-based asyncio loop on Linux, suppose a stream coroutine awaits data that is not yet buffered. Which description matches the readiness path?

options.text: asyncio submits the read to io_uring and the kernel copies the data asynchronously
options.explanation: The default asyncio event loop on Linux uses the `selectors` module (epoll), not io_uring.

options.text: asyncio runs each socket read on a thread in its default executor
options.explanation: Explicit blocking work can use an executor, and some built-in operations such as name resolution also use it. In this default selector socket-read path, receiving data occurs through readiness handling.

options.text: asyncio uses POSIX `aio_read` for sockets
options.explanation: POSIX AIO isn't used by asyncio for sockets, and glibc implements it with threads anyway.

options.text: The event loop registers the socket with epoll, suspends the coroutine, and when epoll reports it readable, performs a synchronous non-blocking `recv()` and resumes the coroutine with the bytes
options.explanation: Correct. It's readiness-based multiplexing. The copy happens synchronously in the event-loop thread; 'async' describes the programming model, not the kernel I/O model.

questions.workedExample:
1. `await reader.read(n)` finds no buffered data, so the transport is waiting on a socket registered with the selector (epoll on Linux).
2. The coroutine is suspended; the loop runs other tasks.
3. The loop calls `epoll_wait`. A packet arrives; epoll reports the fd readable.
4. The loop calls `sock.recv()` on the non-blocking socket. That is a synchronous copy in the loop thread.
5. The data is passed to the protocol and the coroutine is resumed.

Stevens model: I/O multiplexing (model 3).

questions.prompt: You are choosing between a readiness API (epoll) and a completion API (io_uring) for a server with 100,000 mostly idle connections. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A naive design that keeps one pending receive per idle connection must retain each supplied buffer until that operation finishes
options.explanation: Correct. If each of 100,000 requests retains an assumed 16 KiB buffer, their buffer capacity totals 1,562.5 MiB. This is not automatically all resident or pinned. Provided buffers can reduce dedicated per-connection retention, but a shared pool still consumes resources.

options.text: With readiness, a buffer can be allocated only when a socket is reported readable
options.explanation: Correct. This is one reason readiness APIs suited servers with many idle connections.

options.text: Completion APIs can't be used for network sockets, only files
options.explanation: Both IOCP and io_uring handle sockets; IOCP has been used for Windows network servers for decades.

options.text: Readiness APIs can efficiently tell you when a regular file read will complete
options.explanation: For ordinary Linux regular files, readiness does not tell when storage I/O will finish; select/poll commonly report ready and epoll rejects unsupported file types. This is not a universal claim that readiness APIs have no file-related functions.

questions.workedExample:
1. A pending receive using a supplied buffer requires that buffer to remain valid until completion.
2. Assumed capacity: 100,000 × 16 KiB = 1,638,400,000 bytes = 1,562.5 MiB. Residency and pinning depend on API/setup.
3. A readiness design can obtain a buffer when attempting the read.
4. io_uring provided-buffer groups share a pool; availability, ownership and replenishment must be handled. Pool memory is still allocated.
5. Ordinary regular-file readiness on Linux is not storage completion; worker or completion mechanisms can avoid blocking the loop for file I/O.

link.title: Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API — LWN.net

questions.prompt: A Linux team submits many concurrent file reads through glibc POSIX aio_read, expecting no userspace worker threads. Profiling instead finds helper threads executing blocking reads. What explains this?

options.text: POSIX AIO requires `O_DIRECT`, without which it fails with `EINVAL`
options.explanation: glibc POSIX AIO does not require O_DIRECT. Linux native AIO is a different interface, and direct I/O is not itself a guarantee that submission cannot block.

options.text: glibc implements POSIX AIO in user space with a pool of threads making ordinary blocking calls, so it is effectively a thread pool
options.explanation: Correct. glibc uses helper threads for this interface. That explains the execution mechanism; performance relative to a custom pool still requires measurement.

options.text: POSIX AIO only works on sockets
options.explanation: The interface is aimed primarily at files; sockets are usually handled with multiplexing.

options.text: The kernel serialises all AIO requests onto one queue
options.explanation: There's no single kernel queue here at all, because the work is being done by glibc threads in user space.

questions.workedExample:
1. aio_read queues a request in the glibc implementation.
2. A helper thread performs the underlying I/O; excess requests can wait for available workers.
3. Completion status is collected separately through the POSIX AIO interface.
4. aio_init documents a default maximum of 20 workers, adjustable by configuration; a claim of hundreds would require additional evidence.
5. io_uring offers another completion interface but can also use workers. Compare supported operations and measured performance rather than labelling thread-based completion fake.

lessons.title: select, poll and epoll
lessons.summary: How select, poll, epoll and kqueue work inside, why their costs differ, level- versus edge-triggered notification, and how they solved the C10K problem.

questions.prompt: A Linux glibc server built on select corrupts memory after descriptor numbers grow beyond 1023. Which API misuse best explains this?

options.text: `select` returns `EMFILE` above 1,024 descriptors
options.explanation: `EMFILE` comes from the per-process open-file limit, raised by `accept()` or `open()`, not from `select`. And an error wouldn't corrupt memory.

options.text: `FD_SET` on a descriptor ≥ 1024 writes past the end of the fixed-size `fd_set` bitmap, which is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. On Linux glibc `FD_SETSIZE` is 1024. `FD_SET(1050, &set)` sets a bit beyond the structure, scribbling on neighbouring memory. Use poll or epoll.

options.text: The kernel's TCP stack can't handle more than 1,024 connections
options.explanation: The TCP stack is not capped at 1024 sockets by this API; actual capacity depends on resources and configuration.

options.text: `select` scans too slowly and the kernel kills the process
options.explanation: `select` gets slower with more descriptors, but slowness doesn't corrupt memory and the kernel doesn't kill slow processes.

questions.workedExample:
1. `fd_set` is a bitmap of `FD_SETSIZE` bits = 1024 bits = 128 bytes.
2. Descriptor k sets bit k. Valid k: 0 to 1023.
3. At ~1,100 connections, new sockets get numbers above 1023.
4. `FD_SET(1050, &s)` touches byte 1050 / 8 = 131, past the 128-byte struct, typically on the stack.
5. That's a silent buffer overflow. glibc's fortify checks can catch it, but the real fix is `poll` or `epoll`.

questions.prompt: Why must a select loop restore its intended fd_set before each call, either rebuilding it or copying a saved master set?

options.text: Because `select` overwrites the sets on return, leaving only the descriptors that are ready
options.explanation: Correct. The sets are in-out parameters. After the call, bits for non-ready descriptors are cleared, so reusing them would watch only the previously ready ones.

options.text: Because descriptors are renumbered after each call
options.explanation: Descriptor numbers are stable until closed; nothing renumbers them.

options.text: Because `FD_ZERO` resets the kernel's internal list of watched descriptors
options.explanation: `select` keeps no kernel state between calls; the bitmap you pass is the entire interest set every time.

options.text: It doesn't need to; that's only a performance optimisation
options.explanation: Skipping the rebuild is a correctness bug: idle connections silently stop being watched.

questions.workedExample:
Watching fds {4, 5, 6}:

```
before: bits 4,5,6 set
select: fd 5 readable
after:  only bit 5 set
```

If you call `select` again with that same set, you only watch fd 5. Data on 4 or 6 would never be noticed. `poll` avoids this by putting results in a separate `revents` field.

questions.prompt: In an epoll-based server, which call adds a newly accepted connection to the set of descriptors being watched?

options.text: `epoll_wait(ep, evs, 64, -1)`
options.explanation: `epoll_wait` waits for and returns events; it doesn't change what's being watched.

options.text: `epoll_create1(0)`
options.explanation: That creates a new epoll instance. You do it once at start-up, not per connection.

options.text: `epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, &ev)`
options.explanation: Correct. `epoll_ctl` modifies the interest list; `EPOLL_CTL_ADD` inserts the fd with the events in `ev`.

options.text: `poll()` with the new fd appended to the array
options.explanation: That's how you'd do it with `poll`, which keeps no kernel state. epoll's interest list lives in the kernel and is changed with `epoll_ctl`.

questions.workedExample:
epoll splits the job:

1. `epoll_create1`: make the instance (once).
2. `epoll_ctl(ADD/MOD/DEL)`: change the interest list (per connection or per interest change).
3. `epoll_wait`: sleep until events, get the ready ones (in the loop).

After `accept()` returns fd 12, set it non-blocking and call `epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, 12, &ev)`.

questions.prompt: Use a simplified one-scan-per-wake model: 50,000 registered connections, 50 ready candidates per wake, 2,000 wakes per second. Ignoring rescans, contention and registration work, compare poll scan entries with epoll ready-candidate processing.

options.explanation: That treats both as scanning only ready descriptors. poll checks every entry on every call.

options.text: poll: 100 million; epoll: 100 million
options.explanation: epoll doesn't scan the interest list on `epoll_wait`; it takes items off a ready list.

options.text: poll: 50,000; epoll: 50
options.explanation: Those are per-call figures, not per-second. Multiply by 2,000 wake-ups.

options.text: poll: about 100 million; epoll: about 100,000
options.explanation: Correct. poll: 50,000 × 2,000 = 10⁸. epoll: only ready entries, 50 × 2,000 = 10⁵, a thousand times less.

questions.workedExample:
1. poll scan model: 50,000 × 2,000 = 100,000,000 entries/s.
2. epoll candidate model: 50 × 2,000 = 100,000 entries/s.
3. The modeled entry-count ratio is 1,000; it is not a measured CPU-speedup ratio.
4. Assuming an 8-byte pollfd and Linux v6.12 copying behavior: 400,000 input bytes per call → 800 MB/s of input at this rate. The kernel writes 2-byte revents fields, totaling 100,000 output bytes per call → 200 MB/s of result fields, not 800 MB/s each way.

questions.prompt: A non-blocking EPOLLET socket already has all 4 KiB of a request buffered. After receiving the event, the handler reads 1024 bytes and waits only for another epoll event, keeping no local pending-work entry. The peer awaits a response. What correctness risk does this create?

options.text: `epoll_wait` immediately reports the fd again, since 3 KB is still unread
options.explanation: A repeat notification is not guaranteed merely because data remains. This is the behavior an ET application must avoid relying on.

options.text: The connection can stall with 3 KiB unread because another notification is not guaranteed
options.explanation: Correct. Drain until EAGAIN, EOF or error, or keep unfinished work on your own queue so processing can resume without a new kernel notification.

options.text: The kernel discards the unread 3 KB
options.explanation: Unread data stays in the socket's receive buffer; the kernel doesn't drop it.

options.text: `read` returns `EAGAIN` next time and the server closes the connection
options.explanation: A further read would ordinarily find remaining data here. The bug is waiting for a notification that may not recur, rather than attempting that read.

questions.workedExample:
1. The event is delivered with 4096 bytes already buffered.
2. One 1024-byte read leaves 3072 bytes.
3. ET does not guarantee a reminder solely for these remaining bytes, so returning only to epoll_wait can stall the request.
4. Further activity can produce notifications, but correctness cannot depend on that.
5. Continue non-blocking reads to EAGAIN/EOF/error, or enforce fairness with an application pending-work list.

questions.prompt: In the Linux implementation using a red-black-tree epoll interest index, what is the asymptotic cost of the index insertion/search component for N registrations, excluding allocation, locks and target-specific checks?

options.text: O(1), because it is appended to the ready list
options.explanation: Adding to the interest set is not adding to the ready list. A newly added fd goes on the ready list only if it already has events.

options.text: O(N), because the kernel rescans all descriptors
options.explanation: Rescanning is what `poll` does on every call; epoll exists to avoid that.

options.text: O(log N), because the interest list is a red-black tree keyed by file and fd
options.explanation: Correct for the balanced-tree component. Registration can also perform target polling, wait-queue setup, allocation and locking, whose costs are not captured by this tree bound.

options.text: O(N log N), because the tree is re-sorted
options.explanation: Balanced trees insert one element in O(log N) without re-sorting.

questions.workedExample:
1. The interest index distinguishes the pair of open file description and descriptor number.
2. Balanced red-black-tree search/insertion takes O(log N) comparisons.
3. log2(1,000,000) is about 20, indicating scale, not an exact count of comparisons or a bound on total syscall time.
4. Registration includes additional work, and epoll_wait may inspect candidates that no longer produce returned events.

questions.prompt: A level-triggered epoll server registers every connection for `EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT` from the start. CPU sits at 100% even when clients are idle. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: A socket with free send-buffer space is writable almost all the time, so level-triggered `EPOLLOUT` fires on every `epoll_wait`; only register `EPOLLOUT` while there is unsent output
options.explanation: Correct. The loop spins handling 'writable' events with nothing to write. Add `EPOLLOUT` with `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` when a write returns `EAGAIN`, and remove it once the backlog drains.

options.text: `EPOLLIN` and `EPOLLOUT` can't be combined; use two epoll instances
options.explanation: They can be combined in one registration; the problem is level-triggered `EPOLLOUT` on idle sockets.

options.text: Idle TCP connections send keep-alives that wake the loop
options.explanation: Successful keepalive probes are handled within TCP and do not deliver application payload. Keepalive is configurable, often not enabled on a socket at all; persistent writable notifications explain this scenario.

options.text: `epoll_wait` with timeout -1 busy-waits
options.explanation: A timeout of -1 means block indefinitely, which sleeps. The wake-ups come from always-ready `EPOLLOUT`.

questions.workedExample:
1. 'Writable' means the send buffer has space, which is true almost always for an idle connection.
2. Level-triggered: report while the condition holds, so every idle socket is reported every call.
3. `epoll_wait` returns immediately with thousands of `EPOLLOUT` events; the loop does nothing with them and calls again: a spin.
4. Fix: write directly when you have output. If `write` returns `EAGAIN`, `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` to add `EPOLLOUT`; when the buffer drains, remove it.
5. Alternatively use edge-triggered for `EPOLLOUT`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about level-triggered (LT) and edge-triggered (ET) epoll are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: LT keeps a descriptor eligible for reporting while its readiness condition persists
options.explanation: Correct. A particular bounded wait call may return only a subset of ready descriptors, and readiness can change before user code acts.

options.text: ET requires non-blocking descriptors in practice, because you must read until `EAGAIN`
options.explanation: Correct. With a blocking fd, the final read in the drain loop would sleep once the buffer is empty, freezing the loop.

options.text: ET guarantees you never miss data, even if you read only part of it
options.explanation: Wrong way round. ET won't remind you of unread data, so partial reads can stall a connection.

options.text: ET can reduce redundant wake-ups compared with LT
options.explanation: Correct. ET can avoid repeated reports solely because a condition remains true; notification counts and performance still depend on workload and event coalescing.

options.text: LT is incompatible with non-blocking descriptors
options.explanation: LT works fine with non-blocking fds, and event loops normally use them anyway.

questions.workedExample:
1. LT keeps a nonempty socket eligible for reporting; each result batch is limited by maxevents.
2. ET is activity-driven and can coalesce events. It does not promise exactly one event per empty-to-nonempty transition.
3. Leaving unread data may not generate another reminder. Drain to EAGAIN, EOF or error, or keep your own unfinished-work queue.
4. Non-blocking descriptors prevent the drain loop from sleeping when no more bytes are available.

questions.prompt: A server registers socket fd 9 with epoll, then calls `dup(9)`, getting fd 10, and hands fd 10 to a logging subsystem. Later it calls `close(9)` without `EPOLL_CTL_DEL`. What happens when data arrives on that socket?

options.text: Nothing; closing fd 9 removed it from the epoll set
options.explanation: Registrations are removed automatically only when *all* descriptors referring to the open file description are closed. fd 10 still refers to it.

options.text: epoll reports fd 10, because the registration moved to the duplicate
options.explanation: The registration key includes the original fd number and open file description. Its user-supplied data is stored separately and does not automatically change to the duplicate fd.

options.text: The kernel crashes
options.explanation: No crash; this is documented, if surprising, behaviour.

options.text: epoll still reports an event carrying fd 9's registration data, even though fd 9 is closed (and may now be reused for another file)
options.explanation: Correct. epoll tracks the open file description. Since fd 10 keeps it alive, events continue to fire with the old `data`, which may point to freed state or a reused fd number.

questions.workedExample:
1. `epoll_ctl(ADD, 9)` creates an entry keyed by (file description F, fd 9).
2. `dup(9)` → fd 10, also pointing to F.
3. `close(9)` drops one reference; F stays open because of fd 10.
4. epoll only auto-removes the entry when F is finally released, so the entry stays.
5. Data arrives on F → epoll returns an event with the `data` you registered for fd 9.
6. If fd 9 has since been reused for another socket, you'll act on the wrong one. Always `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before `close`.

questions.prompt: Four worker threads all call `epoll_wait` on one shared epoll instance (level-triggered). Occasionally two threads process the same connection at once and its request is parsed out of order. Which change fixes this with the least redesign?

options.text: Switch to `EPOLLET`
options.explanation: Edge-triggered reduces duplicate reports, but a new edge (more data arriving) can still wake a second thread while the first is mid-read. It doesn't guarantee exclusive ownership.

options.text: Register connections with `EPOLLONESHOT` and re-arm with `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` after the handling thread finishes
options.explanation: Correct when one registration and a proper ownership protocol cover the connection. Finish processing before rearming; other I/O paths and duplicate registrations still require coordination.

options.text: Use `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` on every connection
options.explanation: `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` controls wake-ups across *multiple epoll instances* watching one fd. It isn't meant for this, and it doesn't stop a still-ready, level-triggered fd being handed to a second thread waiting on the same instance.

options.text: Call `epoll_wait` with `maxevents = 1`
options.explanation: Each thread then gets one event at a time, but with level-triggered mode a still-readable fd can be handed to another thread straight away.

questions.workedExample:
1. Thread A gets 'fd 42 readable' and starts reading.
2. With LT, fd 42 is still readable, so thread B's `epoll_wait` can return fd 42 too.
3. Both read different chunks: the request is split between threads.
4. `EPOLLONESHOT`: after fd 42 is reported once, epoll disables it.
5. A reads until done, then `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` re-enables fd 42 with `EPOLLIN | EPOLLONESHOT`.
6. The cost is one extra `epoll_ctl` per event.

questions.prompt: A pre-fork server has 32 worker processes, each with its own epoll instance watching the same inherited listening socket. When one connection arrives, all 32 wake up, one wins `accept()`, and 31 get `EAGAIN`. Which fixes address this thundering herd? Pick the best answer.

options.text: Add the listening socket with `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` in each worker, or give each worker its own `SO_REUSEPORT` listening socket so the kernel spreads connections
options.explanation: Correct. `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` (Linux 4.5) wakes one (or a few) of the waiting instances rather than all. `SO_REUSEPORT` (Linux 3.9) gives each worker a separate accept queue, so there's no shared wait at all. nginx supports both.

options.text: Make the listening socket blocking
options.explanation: Blocking `accept()` in 32 processes would avoid busy failures, but those processes couldn't serve their other connections while blocked.

options.text: Switch every worker to `select`
options.explanation: `select` has the same herd problem (and worse scaling).

options.text: Use `EPOLLONESHOT` on the listening socket
options.explanation: One-shot disables the fd per instance after one event, but all 32 instances still get the first event; it also means re-arming after every accept.

questions.workedExample:
1. In the stated scenario a completed connection makes the listening socket readable, waking multiple epoll instances.
2. One worker accepts it; others can find no pending connection and get EAGAIN.
3. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE reduces this herd but documents one or more exclusive waiters, not exactly one. Nonexclusive watchers can still be notified.
4. SO_REUSEPORT gives workers separate listening sockets/queues and distributes flows; it does not guarantee equal application work per worker.
5. Non-blocking accept and correct drain/error handling remain necessary.

questions.prompt: You're porting an epoll server to macOS using kqueue. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: One `kevent()` call can both apply a batch of registration changes and return ready events
options.explanation: Correct. The changelist and eventlist are separate arguments of the same call, whereas epoll needs one `epoll_ctl` syscall per change.

options.text: kqueue can watch process exit, signals and timers directly with filters such as `EVFILT_PROC`, `EVFILT_SIGNAL` and `EVFILT_TIMER`
options.explanation: Correct. Linux achieves the same by turning them into descriptors (`pidfd`, `signalfd`, `timerfd`) and adding those to epoll.

options.text: Edge-triggered behaviour is requested with `EV_CLEAR`
options.explanation: Correct. `EV_CLEAR` resets the filter's state after the event is retrieved, giving edge-like semantics.

options.text: kqueue is completion-based like IOCP, so reads finish in the kernel
options.explanation: kqueue is readiness-based: `EVFILT_READ` tells you data is available (and how many bytes), and you still call `read()`.

questions.workedExample:
Both APIs maintain registrations, but the mapping is conceptual:

| epoll concept | kqueue counterpart |
|---|---|
| create instance | kqueue |
| modify interest | kevent changelist |
| retrieve events | kevent eventlist |
| readable socket | EVFILT_READ |
| edge-like handling | EV_CLEAR, filter-dependent |
| disable after delivery | EV_DISPATCH |
| remove after delivery | EV_ONESHOT |

EPOLLONESHOT disables until MOD rearms; EV_ONESHOT deletes and must be added again. EVFILT_READ is readiness, not a completed socket read.

lessons.title: io_uring
lessons.summary: Linux's completion-based I/O interface, how its shared submission and completion rings work, how it can reduce per-operation overhead, and why Google, Docker and others restrict it.
lessons.body:
epoll reduces repeated interest-set scanning, but applications still perform I/O after readiness notifications. Waits can cover many reads, so the cost is not invariably two syscalls per read. Ordinary regular files do not provide useful storage-completion readiness through epoll. Linux native AIO predates io_uring but has operation/filesystem limitations; O_DIRECT is not a universal requirement or a guarantee of non-blocking submission.

In 2019, Jens Axboe (maintainer of the Linux block layer) merged **io_uring** into Linux 5.1. It is a general-purpose, **completion-based** interface: you describe operations, the kernel performs them, and you collect the results. It covers files, sockets, timers and, by now, a growing, version-dependent set of I/O operations.

## The core idea: two rings in shared memory

An io_uring instance is a pair of **ring buffers** that both the application and the kernel can see, because they are `mmap`ped into the process:

- The **submission queue (SQ)**: the application writes **SQEs** (submission queue entries, normally 64 bytes; optional extended formats exist) describing operations.
- The **completion queue (CQ)**: the kernel writes **CQEs** (completion queue entries, normally 16 bytes; extended formats also exist) with results.

```
   application            kernel
  +-----------+  SQEs  +-----------+
  | writes    | -----> | consumes  |
  | SQ tail   |   SQ   | SQ head   |
  +-----------+        +-----------+
  | reads     | <----- | writes    |
  | CQ head   |   CQ   | CQ tail   |
  +-----------+  CQEs  +-----------+
```

Each ring has a **head** and a **tail**. One side only ever writes the tail (producer), the other only ever advances the head (consumer). In a single-user-producer/consumer design, index publication uses the required memory ordering rather than a userspace mutex. Multiple application threads must coordinate ring access, and kernel completion producers require their own synchronization; this is not a claim that the entire subsystem is lock-free. Ring sizes are powers of two, so the index of entry *i* is `i & (entries - 1)`.

This is the same descriptor-ring-plus-doorbell design that NICs and NVMe drives use (lesson 1), applied between user space and the kernel.

## What's in an entry

An SQE says what to do:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `opcode` | READ, WRITE, ACCEPT, SEND... |
| `fd` | Target descriptor |
| `addr`, `len` | Buffer and length |
| `off` | File offset |
| `user_data` | 64-bit tag, yours |

A CQE gives the result:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user_data` | Copied from the SQE |
| `res` | Like a syscall return; `-errno` on error |
| `flags` | Extra info (e.g. buffer id) |

`user_data` is how you match completions to requests: typically a pointer to your request struct. Completions can arrive **out of order**: a cached read finishes before an earlier one that hit the disk.

## The three system calls

- `io_uring_setup(entries, params)` creates the instance and returns a file descriptor; you `mmap` the rings from it.
- `io_uring_enter(fd, to_submit, min_complete, flags)` tells the kernel "I've added *n* SQEs" and optionally waits for at least *m* completions.
- `io_uring_register(...)` registers long-lived resources: files, buffers, eventfds, restrictions.

Applications commonly use the **liburing** wrappers; direct use requires following the ABI and memory-ordering rules. A minimal single-request liburing fragment follows (supply fd, a 4096-byte buffer, request data and error callbacks):

```c
#include <liburing.h>

struct io_uring ring;
int ret = io_uring_queue_init(
    256, &ring, 0);
if (ret < 0) {
    fail(-ret); exit(1);
}

struct io_uring_sqe *sqe =
    io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
if (!sqe) { fail(ENOSPC); exit(1); }
io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf,
                   4096, 0);
io_uring_sqe_set_data(sqe, req);
ret = io_uring_submit(&ring);
if (ret != 1) {
    fail(ret < 0 ? -ret : EIO); exit(1);
}

struct io_uring_cqe *cqe;
do {
    ret = io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
} while (ret == -EINTR);
if (ret < 0) { fail(-ret); exit(1); }
struct request *r =
    io_uring_cqe_get_data(cqe);
if (cqe->res < 0)
    report(r, -cqe->res);   /* errno */
else
    done(r, cqe->res);      /* bytes */
io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);
io_uring_queue_exit(&ring);
```

Note that errors come back as **negative errno values** in `res`, not via the global `errno`.

## Where overhead can be reduced

### 1. Batching amortises syscalls

With epoll, serving 100 ready sockets is 1 `epoll_wait` plus 100 `read` calls: 101 syscalls. With io_uring you can queue 100 receive SQEs and submit them in **one** `io_uring_enter`, which can also wait for completions in the same call.

Batching amortises syscall overhead. Mitigations, CPU architecture and workload affect the size of the saving; this lesson supplies no universal measured syscall-cost increase.

### 2. SQPOLL: fewer submission syscalls

With `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL`, the kernel starts a thread that **polls the SQ** for new entries. The application just writes SQEs and bumps the tail; the kernel thread picks them up. Completions are read straight from the CQ. In steady state, I/O needs **zero** system calls.

The cost: a kernel thread spinning on a CPU. It goes to sleep after an idle timeout (`sq_thread_idle`), and the application must then wake it with `io_uring_enter` (liburing checks the `IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP` flag for you). It's the polling trade-off from lesson 1 again.

### 3. Registered files and buffers

Ordinary descriptor resolution and resource management have costs, though optimized paths can avoid some reference work. Page pinning is required by some I/O paths, not every buffered copy into user memory. With `io_uring_register` you can pre-register:

- **Fixed files**: refer to them by index; avoid ordinary per-operation descriptor-table resolution while retaining registration/resource bookkeeping.
- **Fixed buffers**: pages pinned once, reused for every `READ_FIXED` and `WRITE_FIXED`.

### 4. Completion interfaces for files

Because it's completion-based, io_uring works for regular files, buffered or `O_DIRECT`, which epoll cannot. Execution depends on opcode, flags and kernel/filesystem support. One common path tries the operation **inline**, then defers if needed:

- For pollable files (sockets, pipes), it arms an internal poll handler and retries when ready. This can avoid dedicating a blocked worker to the wait; threads still execute submission and completion work.
- For things that can't be polled (e.g. a buffered read that misses the page cache on some file systems), it hands the work to an internal pool of kernel workers called **io-wq**.

### 5. Fewer submissions for repetitive work

Newer kernels add features that cut per-operation overhead further:

- **Multishot accept** (5.19) and **multishot receive** (6.0): one SQE produces a stream of CQEs, one per accepted connection or received chunk.
- **Provided buffer rings**: instead of attaching a buffer to every receive up front, the app gives the kernel a pool, and the kernel picks a buffer only when data actually arrives. This can reduce dedicated per-connection buffer retention, but the shared pool still consumes memory and needs capacity/recycling controls.
- **Linked SQEs** (`IOSQE_IO_LINK`): order supported operations without a userspace round trip; errors can cancel subsequent soft links. Linking does not automatically replace a write length with the preceding read's result.
- **Zero-copy send** (`IORING_OP_SEND_ZC`, 6.0).

> [!example] Versioned integration examples
> PostgreSQL 18 documents an optional `io_method = io_uring` backend when built with support. libuv documents `UV_LOOP_USE_IO_URING_SQPOLL`, added in 1.49.0, for supported asynchronous filesystem operations. Availability and defaults depend on the deployed runtime, build and platform; inspect those settings.

## Getting the numbers right

> [!note] Performance evidence gap
> No reproducible benchmark accompanies the original percentage gaps, per-core IOPS figures or workload ranking table. Those claims are omitted. Compare the actual kernel, operation mix, queue depth, CPU budget and storage/network configuration against a measured baseline; batching or polling can help some workloads and hurt others.

## Pitfalls

- **Buffer lifetime.** Keep ordinary read/receive buffers valid until the matching operation completes. For zero-copy send, the first CQE may not release the buffer: if MORE is set, await the notification CQE. Multishot operations and provided-buffer ownership have their own rules.
- **SQE consumption and referenced data lifetimes differ.** Follow each opcode's rules and SUBMIT_STABLE feature behavior; SQPOLL submission return does not necessarily prove the kernel already consumed the SQE. Payload buffers generally live through operation completion.
- **CQ overflow.** If you submit faster than you reap, the CQ can fill. With IORING_FEAT_NODROP, the kernel normally backlogs overflowed CQEs, at a memory/performance cost. Allocation failure can still lose events; NODROP is not an absolute no-loss guarantee. The CQ is twice the SQ size by default for this reason.
- **Cancellation** is asynchronous too (`IORING_OP_ASYNC_CANCEL`); the original operation may still complete.

## Security concerns

io_uring is a large, fast-moving subsystem that runs complex code on behalf of unprivileged processes, and it has had many serious bugs.

- In June 2023, Google reported that **60% of the Linux kernel exploits** submitted to its kCTF vulnerability reward programme in the previous year used io_uring, accounting for about **$1 million** of payouts. The same June 2023 post described then-current restrictions on ChromeOS, production servers and Android apps. This is historical reporting, not proof of every current Google deployment policy.
- The inspected upstream **Moby default seccomp profile** uses an allowlist that omits io_uring syscalls, denying them under that profile. Actual Docker/container policy depends on version, capabilities and the selected profile.
- **Visibility.** A monitor limited to ordinary syscall-entry events does not automatically see one read/open/send syscall per SQE. It may see setup/enter/register calls, while SQPOLL can process submissions without an enter call. Other hooks, audit support and io_uring-aware instrumentation may observe operations; syscall-entry visibility alone is not a complete security model.

Mitigations:

- `sysctl kernel.io_uring_disabled` (Linux 6.6): `0` allows everyone, `1` limits creation to privileged processes or members of the `kernel.io_uring_group` group, and `2` disables new ring creation for everyone. Existing rings remain usable under either restrictive value.
- `IORING_REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS` lets a process constrain opcodes/flags on a ring created with IORING_SETUP_R_DISABLED, before enabling and handing it to less trusted code. It is an allowlist, not a complete sandbox by itself.
- Seccomp can block `io_uring_setup` altogether.

> [!warning] Know your deployment target
> If you build on io_uring, check that your production environment allows it. Many container platforms and hardened kernels do not, so keep an epoll or thread-pool fallback.

## Key takeaways
- io_uring is completion-based: the application writes SQEs into a shared submission ring and reaps CQEs from a shared completion ring, matched by `user_data`.
- Shared rings can reduce submission/completion transfer overhead; correct ordering and concurrent-access coordination remain necessary. Payload copying is a separate issue.
- Gains come from batching, SQPOLL (no syscalls in steady state), registered files and buffers, completion-based file I/O and multishot operations.
- Errors arrive as negative errno in `cqe->res`, completions can be out of order, and buffer lifetime follows the operation, including zero-copy-send notification and multishot rules.
- Historical vulnerabilities motivated deployment restrictions. Check actual container policy and instrumentation; kernel.io_uring_disabled controls new ring creation rather than revoking existing rings.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: In io_uring, which side writes entries into the **completion queue (CQ)**?

options.text: The kernel produces completion entries according to the operation and flags
options.explanation: Correct. Normal CQEs are 16 bytes, with optional formats. Multishot operations can emit several CQEs, successful CQEs can sometimes be suppressed, and zero-copy sends can emit a later buffer-release notification.

options.text: The application, after it finishes processing a request
options.explanation: The application only consumes the CQ (advancing its head). Writing results is the kernel's job; the application writes to the SQ.

options.text: liburing, by copying results out of the SQ
options.explanation: liburing is a thin user-space wrapper. It does not produce completions; the SQ holds requests, not results.

options.text: Both sides, protected by a shared mutex
options.explanation: The logical producer/consumer roles do not imply every execution context is a single thread. Application sharing requires synchronization, and the kernel coordinates completion production.

questions.workedExample: SQ: application publishes requests, kernel consumes them. CQ: kernel publishes results, application consumes them. Publication uses defined memory ordering. Coordinate multiple userspace threads rather than assuming the entire subsystem is lock-free. CQE count and size depend on opcode and setup flags.

questions.prompt: A completion arrives with `cqe->res == -2`. What does it mean?

options.text: 2 bytes were transferred
options.explanation: Byte counts are non-negative. A negative `res` always signals an error.

options.text: Check the global `errno` for the real error
options.explanation: Per-operation failure is encoded directly in cqe->res. Many liburing APIs also return negative errno directly rather than setting the C errno variable; check the called function's contract.

options.text: The operation failed with errno 2 (`ENOENT`)
options.explanation: Correct. io_uring reports errors as negative errno values in `res`, so -2 is `-ENOENT`, e.g. an `openat` on a missing path.

options.text: The CQ overflowed and 2 completions were lost
options.explanation: Overflow is signalled through ring flags and the kernel's backlog, not through a single CQE's `res`.

questions.workedExample:
1. `res` behaves like a syscall return value.
2. Success: `res >= 0` (bytes read, new fd, etc.).
3. Failure: `res = -errno`.
4. -2 → errno 2 → `ENOENT` (no such file or directory).

So `report(r, -cqe->res)` turns it back into a positive errno for `strerror`.

questions.prompt: Why does every SQE carry a 64-bit `user_data` field?

options.text: It tells the kernel which CPU to run the operation on
options.explanation: CPU placement isn't controlled per SQE this way; `user_data` is opaque to the kernel.

options.text: It is a checksum the kernel uses to validate the entry
options.explanation: It is not a checksum. The application chooses a tag that is returned with completions; some operations such as cancellation can also use user_data as an identifier to match pending work.

options.text: It sets the operation's priority in the queue
options.explanation: Priority uses a separate `ioprio` field; `user_data` is purely for the application.

options.text: So the application can match each CQE to its request, because completions may arrive out of order
options.explanation: Correct. The kernel copies `user_data` unchanged into the CQE. Typically it holds a pointer to your request struct.

questions.workedExample:
Submit three reads A, B, C in order. A misses the page cache and goes to disk; B and C are cached.

```
CQ order: B, C, A
```

Without a tag you couldn't tell which result belongs to which buffer. Set `user_data = (u64)req` on submit and read it back with `io_uring_cqe_get_data(cqe)`.

questions.prompt: In a simplified successful batch, one epoll_wait returns 100 readable sockets and each needs one read. For io_uring, assume 100 receives fit in the ring and one enter call submits and waits for all 100 completions without interruption. Excluding setup and retries, compare syscall counts.

options.text: epoll: 2; io_uring: 100
options.explanation: epoll needs one `read` per socket after the single `epoll_wait`, so it's far more than 2. And io_uring batches, so it's not 100.

options.text: epoll: 101; io_uring: about 1
options.explanation: Correct. epoll: 1 `epoll_wait` + 100 `read`. io_uring: the 100 SQEs go in one `io_uring_enter`, which can also wait for completions.

options.text: Both about 101: io_uring still needs one syscall per operation
options.explanation: That's the misconception io_uring was built to fix. Submissions are batched through the shared ring.

options.text: epoll: 100; io_uring: 0
options.explanation: Without SQPOLL, io_uring still needs `io_uring_enter` to submit and/or wait. Zero syscalls requires a kernel polling thread.

questions.workedExample:
1. Stated epoll path: one wait plus 100 reads = 101 syscalls.
2. Stated io_uring path: publish 100 SQEs, then one io_uring_enter requesting submission and waiting for 100 completions.
3. Reap the 100 CQEs from shared memory.
4. Waiting for only one completion does not guarantee all 100 are ready; real paths may require more waits, handle partial submissions, interruptions or other progress work. This is a syscall-count model, not a benchmark.

link.title: Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API — LWN.net

questions.prompt: An SQPOLL ring has no pending work. After its poller exceeds the configured idle timeout and sleeps, an application publishes a new SQE but omits the documented wakeup check. Why may it remain unprocessed?

options.text: SQPOLL only works for files opened with `O_DIRECT`
options.explanation: SQPOLL is submission polling, not the IOPOLL completion mode whose read/write paths require supported direct I/O. Opcode/setup restrictions still depend on kernel version.

options.text: The SQ is full and the entry was dropped
options.explanation: An idle ring isn't full. And a full SQ means `io_uring_get_sqe` returns NULL; it doesn't drop silently.

options.text: The kernel polling thread went to sleep after `sq_thread_idle`; the app must check `IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP` and call `io_uring_enter` to wake it
options.explanation: Correct. The poller sleeps when idle to stop burning a CPU. liburing's `io_uring_submit` checks the flag and wakes it for you.

options.text: SQPOLL requires a syscall for every SQE
options.explanation: The point of SQPOLL is that steady-state submissions need no syscall at all.

questions.workedExample:
SQPOLL is a polling trade-off:

1. Busy: a kernel thread spins on the SQ tail, picking up SQEs with no syscalls.
2. Idle for `sq_thread_idle` ms: the thread sleeps and sets `IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP` in the SQ flags.
3. New work: the app must see the flag and call `io_uring_enter` with `IORING_ENTER_SQ_WAKEUP`.

If you hand-roll the ring and skip step 3, submissions sit there unprocessed.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms can reduce io_uring overhead for suitable workloads and supported configurations? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many operations submitted in one `io_uring_enter`
options.explanation: Correct. Batching amortises the fixed syscall cost, which grew after the Spectre/Meltdown mitigations.

options.text: Registered files avoid ordinary per-operation descriptor-table resolution
options.explanation: Correct. Registration retains file resources and permits indexed use, reducing ordinary descriptor resolution/reference overhead; it does not eliminate all bookkeeping.

options.text: Registered buffers are pinned once rather than per operation
options.explanation: Correct for supported fixed-buffer operations. Registration can amortize pinning/mapping work; ordinary buffered copies do not universally pin pages per operation.

options.text: The kernel skips the copy from kernel to user space for every read
options.explanation: Ordinary io_uring reads still copy data into your buffer. Zero-copy needs specific features (e.g. `SEND_ZC` for sends); it isn't the default.

options.text: SQPOLL can remove syscalls entirely in steady state
options.explanation: Correct, at the cost of a kernel thread spinning on a CPU.

questions.workedExample: Batching can amortize submission costs; registered resources can amortize appropriate lookup/pinning costs; SQPOLL can remove steady-state submission syscalls when its thread remains active. These are mechanisms, not guaranteed speedups. An ordinary buffered read still copies payload, whereas direct I/O or specific zero-copy features follow different paths.

link.title: Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API — LWN.net

questions.prompt: Why can io_uring expose a completion interface for supported buffered regular-file reads when epoll readiness does not report their storage completion?

options.text: epoll returns an error for regular files, but io_uring converts them to sockets
options.explanation: Nothing is converted. (In fact epoll rejects regular files with `EPERM`.)

options.text: io_uring reads files with `O_DIRECT` automatically
options.explanation: io_uring supports both buffered and `O_DIRECT` I/O; it doesn't force `O_DIRECT`.

options.text: epoll is slower on files because of the 1024-fd limit
options.explanation: The 1024 limit belongs to `select`, not epoll, and it's unrelated to files versus sockets.

options.text: Regular files are always 'ready' for readiness APIs, so epoll can't tell you a read would block; io_uring is completion-based and can hand blocking work to its io-wq workers
options.explanation: Correct in principle. A completion request can finish inline, through supported asynchronous paths or through io-wq workers. The path varies with opcode, flags, filesystem and kernel version.

questions.workedExample:
1. Readiness model: 'tell me when a read won't block'. A disk file is always considered readable, even if the page isn't cached, so the read can still block.
2. Completion model: 'do this read and tell me when it's done'.
3. io_uring's path: try non-blocking inline → if it would block on a pollable fd, arm poll → otherwise queue to io-wq → post a CQE when done.

That's why Node.js historically needed a thread pool for files.

options.text: Nothing: the kernel copied `buf` into the SQE at submit
options.explanation: The SQE holds only the buffer's address and length, not its contents. Data is written there later.

options.text: Memory corruption: the kernel may write received data into that stack memory after the function returns
options.explanation: Correct. The buffer must stay valid until the matching CQE arrives. Use heap memory owned by the request struct.

options.text: A compile error, because `buf` is on the stack
options.explanation: It compiles fine; that's what makes the bug dangerous.

options.text: The recv fails with `EFAULT` immediately
options.explanation: The request is pending in this scenario. Later access might corrupt reused stack memory or fail depending on mapping changes; immediate EFAULT is not a guaranteed safeguard.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
t0 submit recv(buf=0x7ffd..)
t1 function returns; stack reused
t2 packet arrives
t3 kernel writes into 0x7ffd..
```

At t3 the kernel scribbles over whatever now lives at that address. Rule: a buffer belongs to the kernel from submit until its CQE is reaped.

questions.prompt: A server hypothetically retains one **16 KiB** buffer for each of 50,000 pending receives, totaling 781.25 MiB of buffer capacity. Which feature can reduce per-connection retention by drawing from a smaller shared pool?

options.text: SQPOLL
options.explanation: SQPOLL removes submission syscalls; it doesn't change how many buffers are committed.

options.text: Linked SQEs
options.explanation: Links chain dependent operations; they don't reduce buffer memory.

options.text: Provided buffer rings, so the kernel picks a buffer from a shared pool only when data actually arrives
options.explanation: Correct. Provided buffers decouple dedicated buffer ownership from every idle receive. Size the pool for outstanding data and processing lifetime, and handle exhaustion/replenishment; pending receives do not inherently mean every byte is physically pinned.

options.text: Registered files
options.explanation: Fixed files save the fd lookup cost, not buffer memory.

questions.workedExample:
1. 50,000 × 16 KiB = 819,200,000 bytes = 781.25 MiB of capacity, not necessarily the same RSS.
2. An illustrative shared pool of 1,024 such buffers uses 16 MiB.
3. Receive completion flags identify selected buffers. Recycle only after application processing and kernel-use rules allow it.
4. The smaller pool can exhaust during bursts; handle ENOBUFS/termination behavior and replenish/rearm as the operation requires.

questions.prompt: Which statements about documented io_uring deployment restrictions and syscall-entry monitoring are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The inspected upstream Moby default seccomp allowlist omits io_uring syscalls
options.explanation: Correct for that profile. Actual container policy depends on the selected runtime version/profile and configuration; changing the profile is not the only possible prerequisite.

options.text: Monitoring only ordinary syscall-entry events does not automatically expose every SQE as a separate read/open/send syscall
options.explanation: Correct. Ring operations require suitable instrumentation; setup/register/enter can be visible, and other hooks may observe operations. SQPOLL need not enter once per submission.

options.text: In its June 2023 post, Google reported about 60% of prior-year kCTF exploit submissions used io_uring
options.explanation: Correct as dated reporting. It does not establish the same proportion or deployment policy today.

options.text: io_uring requires root, so containers would need privileged mode
options.explanation: By default unprivileged processes can create rings. Linux 6.6's `kernel.io_uring_disabled=1` can restrict it, but that's opt-in.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check the actual profile: the inspected Moby allowlist does not include io_uring setup/enter/register calls.
2. A syscall-entry-only monitor does not automatically see one syscall for every ring operation; other instrumentation may.
3. The 60% statistic belongs to Google's June 2023 historical report, not a current universal rate.
4. Unprivileged ring creation is possible when policy permits; kernel settings and seccomp can restrict it.
